meta.title: Ancient Civilizations
meta.subtitle: Europe, the Mediterranean, Africa, the Near East, Iran, the Steppe, South and East Asia, and the Americas, c. 3500–330 BCE
meta.description: Bronze Age and early Iron Age civilizations: Europe, the western Mediterranean, North Africa, Nubia, Africa south of the Sahara, the Aegean and Greece, Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt, Mesopotamia and Assyria, Iran, the Eurasian Steppe, South Asia, mainland Southeast Asia, China, Korea and Japan, and the Americas.
meta.credits: Dates and events come from English Wikipedia (read 17 November 2026) and the scholarly works it cites; each event lists its sources. Ancient dates are uncertain and scholars disagree. The lighter parts of a bar show the range of dates the cited sources give for its start and end, and the chronology menus re-plot a region under another dating system. Compiled with AI assistance and not yet reviewed by a specialist.

middle.name: Middle Chronology
middle.description: Fall of Babylon in 1595 BCE; Hammurabi reigns 1792–1750 BCE. Wikipedia calls it the most commonly seen solution, 'but there is far from a consensus'.

source.sourceLocation: Middle Bronze Age; table 'Variant Middle Bronze Age chronologies'

high.name: High (Long) Chronology
high.description: Fall of Babylon in 1651 BCE: 56 years earlier than the Middle Chronology. Applied here to dates before 1400 BCE (see docs/ancient-sources.md).

low.name: Low (Short) Chronology
low.description: Fall of Babylon in 1531 BCE: 64 years later than the Middle Chronology. Where a source gives its own short-chronology date, that date is used instead of the shift.

egypt-c14.name: Radiocarbon
egypt-c14.description: Radiocarbon dates for the starts of dynasties (Bronk Ramsey et al. 2010 and related work), as tabulated by Wikipedia.

aegean-high.name: High (radiocarbon) Aegean chronology
aegean-high.description: Absolute dates for the Minoan and Helladic phases based on radiocarbon (Manning 2012), with the Thera eruption in the late 17th or 16th century BCE.

aegean-low.name: Low (conventional) Aegean chronology
aegean-low.description: Dates from archaeological synchronisms with Egypt, roughly a century later for the eruption and early Late Bronze Age phases.

xszcp.name: Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project
xszcp.description: Dates from the Chinese government project commissioned in 1996: Xia c. 2070–1600 BCE, Shang c. 1600–1046 BCE, the Zhou conquest in 1046 BCE. Doubts persist on these dates, and many Western scholars consider the Xia unproven.

liu-xin.name: Traditional (Liu Xin)
liu-xin.description: The traditional chronology computed by Liu Xin (1st century BCE): Xia 2205–1766 BCE, the Zhou conquest in 1122 BCE.

events.title: Urukean expansion
events.descr: The peak of Uruk's influence in the Late Uruk phase: colonies and trading posts far beyond southern Mesopotamia, monumental building and administrative record-keeping.

sources.sourceLocation: Outline of the 4th millennium BC in the Near East

events.title: Earliest proto-cuneiform tablets (Uruk IV)
events.descr: Administrative tablets from Uruk's Eanna district, the earliest stage of the writing that became cuneiform. Dates are the CDLI's, as cited by Wikipedia.

sources.sourceLocation: Outline of the 4th millennium BC (CDLI, Uruk IV)

events.title: Royal tombs of Ur
events.descr: The richly furnished royal burials of Ur, including the Standard of Ur, belong to Early Dynastic IIIa.

events.title: Lugal-zage-si unites Sumer
events.descr: King of Umma, then of Uruk. He ended Umma's long border war with Lagash and ruled Ur, Nippur, Larsa and Kish: the last Sumerian king before Akkadian rule. The reign dates are from the article's navbox and carry no footnote.

sources.sourceLocation: Reign; navbox '3rd dynasty of Uruk, 2358–2334 BC'

events.title: Reign of Sargon of Akkad
events.descr: Founder of the Akkadian Empire, often called the first empire. Within the middle chronology, scholars offer several reign dates; all are recorded here.

events.title: Sargon conquers Sumer
events.descr: Sargon defeats Lugal-zage-si, takes Uruk and brings the Sumerian cities under Akkad; later campaigns reach Elam and Mari.

events.title: Reign of Naram-Sin
events.descr: Sargon's grandson. He took the title 'King of the Four Corners', was the first Mesopotamian king to claim divinity in his lifetime, and campaigned as far as Anatolia and Ebla.

events.title: Fall of Akkad and Gutian rule
events.descr: After weak successors, Akkadian rule ends and Gutian kings based at Adab hold sway in Sumer.

events.title: Utu-hengal of Uruk defeats the Gutians
events.descr: Utu-hengal defeats the Gutian king Tirigan and restores Sumerian kingship, only to be ousted by Ur-Nammu about eight years later.

source.sourceLocation: end of Gutian rule, c. 2119 BC

startDates.note: The page gives both dates without naming a chronology; the later one matches the low chronology.

events.title: Ur-Nammu founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
events.descr: Ur-Nammu takes the titles King of Ur and King of Sumer and Akkad. The Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest surviving law code, is attributed to him (Wikipedia gives it no date).

events.title: Reign of Shulgi
events.descr: Ur-Nammu's son reigns for about half the dynasty's length, consolidating the kingdom into an empire on the Akkadian model.

events.title: Elamites destroy Ur
events.descr: A coalition from Anshan and Shimashki deals the final blow to the Third Dynasty of Ur under Ibbi-Sin; Ur is destroyed. Isin and Larsa rise in its place.

source.sourceLocation: lead (low chronology end of Ur III)

events.title: Sumu-abum makes Babylon independent
events.descr: The Amorite chieftain Sumu-abum founds the First Dynasty of Babylon.

events.title: Reign of Hammurabi
events.descr: The sixth king of Babylon reigns 43 years, conquers Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari, and issues his law code. His reign is the usual reference point for the competing chronologies.

events.title: Hammurabi conquers Larsa
events.descr: Babylon defeats Rim-Sin I of Larsa in Hammurabi's 30th year, gaining Nippur, Ur, Uruk and Isin and ending the Isin–Larsa period.

events.title: Hammurabi takes Eshnunna and Mari
events.descr: Eshnunna falls in 1762 and Mari in 1761; Mari's palace is burned, preserving its great archive (1774–1761 BCE).

events.title: Code of Hammurabi
events.descr: The basalt stele of nearly 300 laws, compiled late in Hammurabi's reign. It was later carried off to Susa as plunder, where it was found in 1901.

events.title: Assyrian merchant colony at Kanesh (kārum level II)
events.descr: Old Assyrian merchants trade tin and textiles from a quarter outside the Anatolian city of Kanesh, leaving thousands of tablets. The level ends in a fire.

sources.sourceLocation: Archaeology ('Mesopotamian middle chronology according to Veenhof')

events.title: Trade revives at Kanesh (kārum level Ib)
events.descr: Trade is rebuilt, under the control of Ishme-Dagan I of Assyria, until the colony burns again.

events.title: Reign of Anitta of Kussara
events.descr: Anitta takes Neša (Kanesh) after his father Pithana, defeats Zalpuwa, sacks Hattusa and makes Neša his capital. His inscription is among the oldest texts in Hittite.

events.title: Anitta burns Hattusa
events.descr: A burnt layer at Hattusa is credited to Anitta, who cursed anyone who would resettle the site. The Hittite kings later made it their capital.

events.title: Reign of Ḫattušili I; the capital moves to Hattusa
events.descr: The earliest Hittite king with contemporary records takes the name 'the man of Hattusa', moves his capital there and campaigns into Syria.

source.sourceLocation: p. 25 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)
p. 25 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)

events.title: Alalakh's Level VII palace destroyed
events.descr: Dated by the excavator to the second year of Ḫattušili I's reign, during his Syrian campaigns.

events.title: Reign of Mursili I
events.descr: Ḫattušili's grandson renews the Syrian wars, takes Aleppo and raids Babylon. He is assassinated on his return by a conspiracy led by Ḫantili I and Zidanta I.

source.sourceLocation: p. 25 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)
p. 25 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)

events.title: Mursili I takes Aleppo
events.descr: The Hittites conquer Yamhad and its capital Aleppo before marching about 2,000 km down the Euphrates to Babylon.

events.title: Hittite sack of Babylon
events.descr: Mursili I raids Babylon and ends the dynasty of Hammurabi. The raid wasn't meant to hold territory; the Kassites take control afterwards. This date anchors the competing Mesopotamian chronologies.

events.title: Kassites take power in Babylonia
events.descr: A people from the Zagros mountains take Babylonia after the Hittite raid and rule it for over four centuries.

events.title: Telepinu Proclamation
events.descr: King Telepinu's edict sets rules for the royal succession after generations of murders. Little more than the names of his successors is known for about 80 years.

events.title: Kirta, first king of Mitanni
events.descr: The Hurrian kingdom of Mitanni rises in northern Syria and south-eastern Anatolia, between the Hittites, Egypt, the Kassites and Assyria.

events.title: Reign of Šuppiluliuma I
events.descr: The Hittite empire's great expansion: Mitanni is broken in the One-Year and Six-Year wars, Carchemish is taken, and Hatti becomes a great power that writes to Egypt in the Amarna letters.

source.sourceLocation: via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings (Bryce column)
via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings
via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings

events.title: Ashur-uballit I of Assyria takes Mitanni lands
events.descr: Assyria breaks free of Mitanni and, in the middle of the 14th century, annexes Mitanni territory. Wikipedia notes the Assyrian King List is considered roughly correct from his reign on.

events.title: Reign of Muwatalli II
events.descr: Muwatalli moves the royal seat south to Tarḫuntašša and faces Ramesses II at Kadesh.

sources.sourceLocation: lead (Van De Mieroop 2007, p. 159); Move to Tarhuntassa

source.sourceLocation: via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings

events.title: Battle of Kadesh
events.descr: Ramesses II and Muwatalli II fight on the Orontes in Ramesses's fifth year; both claim victory and the result is a stalemate. Possibly the largest chariot battle ever fought.

startDates.note: 'the high chronology has the date about 20 years earlier'

events.title: Reign of Ḫattušili III
events.descr: Muwatalli's brother, the Hittite commander at Kadesh, deposes his nephew Mursili III (Urhi-Teshub) and makes peace with Egypt.

events.title: Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty
events.descr: Ramesses II and Ḫattušili III agree the earliest surviving peace treaty, about fifteen years after Kadesh. Egyptian and Hittite versions both survive.

source.sourceLocation: body ('the 21st year of Ramesses II's reign (1258 BC)')

events.title: Ramesses II marries a daughter of Ḫattušili III
events.descr: A diplomatic marriage in Ramesses's 34th year seals the peace.

events.title: Reign of Tudḫaliya IV
events.descr: Ḫattušili's son loses to Assyria at Nihriya and claims a conquest of Alashiya (Cyprus).

source.sourceLocation: via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings
via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings

events.title: Battle of Nihriya
events.descr: Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria defeats Tudḫaliya IV over the remnants of Mitanni: the first direct defeat of the Hittites by Assyria.

events.title: Assyria annexes what is left of Mitanni (Ḫanigalbat)
events.descr: Under Shalmaneser I the rump Mitanni state, long passed between Hittite and Assyrian control, is finally annexed. The year isn't known; the bar spans his reign.

events.title: Reign of Šuppiluliuma II, last Hittite great king
events.descr: He campaigns against Tarḫuntašša and wins what is described as the first recorded naval battle, off Cyprus. He probably left Hattusa; the old story that he died in its sack is now doubted.

events.title: Hattusa abandoned and burned
events.descr: The Hittite capital is abandoned over several decades; the final fire probably came after the court had left. A severe drought is one suspected cause.

events.title: Neo-Hittite (Syro-Hittite) states
events.descr: Luwian and Aramean successor kingdoms such as Carchemish keep Hittite traditions alive in south-eastern Anatolia and Syria until Assyria absorbs them; Carchemish falls in 717 BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: Late Bronze Age – Early Iron Age transition ('12th century BCE')

source.sourceLocation: infobox (end of Hattusa, after which the states arose)

events.title: Troy VI destroyed
events.descr: The final sublayer of the great Middle–Late Bronze Age citadel (Troy VI, built c. 1750) is destroyed; Troy VIIa is built soon after.

events.title: Troy VIIa destroyed
events.descr: The city is destroyed around the time of the Late Bronze Age collapse; often discussed as a candidate for Homer's Troy.

events.title: Three-year drought in central Anatolia
events.descr: Tree rings show severe drought in 1198, 1197 and 1196 BCE, suggested as a factor in the Hittite collapse.

events.title: Narmer unifies Egypt
events.descr: Narmer, shown on the Narmer Palette and widely identified with Menes, is credited with conquering Lower Egypt and founding the First Dynasty. His date carries a margin of about 150 years.

events.title: Djoser and the Step Pyramid
events.descr: The first king of the Third Dynasty; his architect Imhotep is credited with the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first large stone pyramid.

events.title: Khufu builds the Great Pyramid
events.descr: Khufu's pyramid at Giza, built over about 26 years, stays the tallest structure on Earth for thousands of years. The bar is Khufu's reign; other dating systems put it decades apart.

sources.sourceLocation: Height of the Old Kingdom ('Khufu (2589–2566 BC)')
lead; Historiographical record (table of reign dates)

source.sourceLocation: via Wikipedia: Great Pyramid of Giza (table)
via Wikipedia: Great Pyramid of Giza (table)
'2613–2577 BC' (via Wikipedia: Great Pyramid of Giza)

events.title: Mentuhotep II reunites Egypt
events.descr: The Theban king takes the throne, captures Herakleopolis in his 14th year and completes reunification by his 39th, founding the Middle Kingdom.

sources.sourceLocation: Reunification under the Eleventh Dynasty ('ascended the Theban throne in 2055 BC')

events.title: Senusret III's funerary boat (tree-ring dated)
events.descr: Dendrochronology dates the boat's timber to 1887 ± 11 BCE, an independent check on the conventional reign of Senusret III (1878–1839 BCE).

events.title: Hyksos rule from Avaris (15th Dynasty)
events.descr: Rulers of Levantine origin hold the north of Egypt from Avaris while Theban dynasties rule the south. Scholars' dates for the dynasty differ by a few decades.

events.title: Ahmose I expels the Hyksos
events.descr: After three failed attacks, Ahmose takes Avaris and then Sharuhen after a three-year siege, reuniting Egypt and opening the New Kingdom.

events.title: Reign of Ahmose I
events.descr: Founder of the 18th Dynasty. Published reign dates range over about thirty years; radiocarbon puts his accession at 1570–1544 BCE.

source.sourceLocation: p. 1556 (via Wikipedia: Ahmose I), 95% range 1570–1544 BC

events.title: Egyptian annals mention Tanaju (Danaans?)
events.descr: Messengers from Tanaju appear in Thutmose III's annals, a possible early Egyptian reference to Mycenaean Greeks.

events.title: Reign of Hatshepsut
events.descr: Regent for Thutmose III, then pharaoh in her own right from about her seventh year. She builds at Karnak and Deir el-Bahari and sends a trading expedition to Punt.

events.title: Expedition to Punt
events.descr: In Hatshepsut's ninth year a trading fleet sails to Punt; the voyage is recorded in reliefs at Deir el-Bahari.

events.title: Reign of Thutmose III
events.descr: Co-ruler with Hatshepsut, then sole king and Egypt's great empire-builder in the Levant.

events.title: Battle of Megiddo
events.descr: Thutmose III defeats a Canaanite coalition and besieges Megiddo for seven months: the first battle recorded in reasonably reliable detail.

source.sourceLocation: 'other publications place the battle in 1482 BC or 1479 BC'

events.title: Reign of Akhenaten
events.descr: The pharaoh who promotes the worship of the Aten, changes his name in his fifth year and builds a new capital at Akhetaten (Amarna).

events.title: Amarna period and the Amarna letters
events.descr: Akhetaten is Egypt's capital. Its archive of 382 cuneiform tablets holds letters between the pharaohs and the kings of Babylon, Mitanni, Hatti and Assyria, covering no more than 30 years in the mid-14th century.

events.title: Reign of Tutankhamun
events.descr: The boy king restores the worship of Amun and returns the court to Memphis. His nearly intact tomb (KV62) was found in 1922.

events.title: Reign of Ramesses II
events.descr: A reign of 66 years: Kadesh, the peace with the Hittites, and building from Abu Simbel to the Ramesseum. Most Egyptologists date his accession to 31 May 1279 BCE; older high and middle Egyptian chronologies put it earlier.

source.sourceLocation: 1995, p. 205 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)
1995, p. 205 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)

events.title: Reign of Merneptah; war with Libyans and Sea Peoples
events.descr: Ramesses II's successor defeats a Libyan invasion joined by groups of Sea Peoples, recorded in the Great Karnak Inscription.

events.title: Battle of the Delta
events.descr: In his eighth year Ramesses III defeats the Sea Peoples at the mouths of the Nile, the best-recorded of their invasions (Medinet Habu).

sources.sourceLocation: lead; infobox; footnotes 1–2 (Drews 2020, p. 51; Beckman 2000, p. 23)

events.title: Shoshenq I founds the 22nd Dynasty
events.descr: A Libyan dynasty takes the throne at Bubastis; Shoshenq campaigns in the Levant.

events.title: Kushite (25th) Dynasty
events.descr: Kings from Kush (Nubia) conquer Egypt, beginning with Piye's march north around 732 BCE, and rule until the Assyrian invasions.

events.title: Assyrian invasions of Egypt
events.descr: Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal defeat the Kushite kings; in 664 BCE the Assyrians sack Thebes and Memphis.

sources.sourceLocation: End of the Third Intermediate Period ('over the period 670–663 BC')

events.title: Assyrians sack Thebes
events.descr: The sack of Egypt's religious capital ends Kushite rule in Egypt.

events.title: Psamtik I reunites Egypt (26th Dynasty)
events.descr: A former Assyrian vassal at Sais, Psamtik (reigned 664–610 BCE) brings Thebes under his rule and Egypt back to independence: the Saite period.

events.title: Battle of Pelusium: Persia conquers Egypt
events.descr: Cambyses II defeats Psamtik III and Egypt becomes a Persian province, beginning the First Achaemenid Period (525–404 BCE).

events.title: First Minoan palaces built
events.descr: The first palaces rise at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia on earlier ceremonial sites; the potter's wheel and Kamares ware appear.

events.title: Linear A in use
events.descr: The undeciphered Minoan script of palace administration and religion, later adapted into Linear B.

events.title: First palaces destroyed
events.descr: Mass destructions, usually blamed on earthquakes, end the Protopalatial period; the palaces are rebuilt larger.

events.title: Shaft graves of Grave Circle A, Mycenae
events.descr: Six rich shaft graves holding 19 bodies, among them the gold 'Mask of Agamemnon'; the cemetery is later enclosed within the citadel.

events.title: Thera (Minoan) eruption
events.descr: A huge eruption buries Akrotiri and sends a tsunami to Crete, late in LM IA. Radiocarbon puts it in the late 17th or 16th century BCE; archaeological synchronisms with Egypt suggest about a century later. The exact year is unsettled.

sources.sourceLocation: prose on high and low chronologies

source.sourceLocation: 1627–1600 BC, olive-tree wiggle-match (via Wikipedia: Minoan eruption)
radiocarbon table: Pearson et al. 2023, 1610–1510 BC (95.4%, IntCal20)

events.title: LM IB destructions across Crete
events.descr: Island-wide destructions, apparently deliberate, end the Neopalatial period; at Knossos the town burns but the palace survives.

sources.sourceLocation: Second Palace period ('partially destroyed around 1450 BC')

events.title: Mycenaeans at Knossos; Linear B appears
events.descr: Knossos becomes a Mycenaean administrative centre keeping its records in Linear B, the earliest written Greek.

events.title: Linear B in use
events.descr: The Mycenaean palace script, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952.

events.title: Uluburun shipwreck
events.descr: A merchant ship sinks off southern Anatolia with ten tons of copper, tin, glass and luxury goods: a snapshot of Late Bronze Age trade between Egypt, the Levant, Cyprus and the Aegean.

events.title: Palace of Knossos destroyed
events.descr: A major fire destroys the Mycenaean-era palace; the date is conventional and still debated.

events.title: Lion Gate and citadel walls at Mycenae
events.descr: Mycenae's fortifications are extended to take in Grave Circle A, and the Lion Gate is built.

events.title: Palace of Nestor at Pylos burns
events.descr: The best-preserved Mycenaean palace burns, baking its Linear B archive. Wikipedia's articles give dates from about 1250 to 1180 BCE.

source.sourceLocation: Blegen's dating, end of LH IIIB

events.title: Late Bronze Age collapse
events.descr: Across the eastern Mediterranean, palace economies fail: the Hittite state ends, Mycenaean palaces burn, Ugarit falls, and Egypt fights off the Sea Peoples. Drought, earthquakes, raids and the breakdown of trade are all proposed causes.

events.title: Sub-Mycenaean period
events.descr: The last traces of Mycenaean culture as Greece enters the Iron Age.

events.title: Greek Dark Ages
events.descr: A period of smaller settlements, no writing and little long-distance trade, until the rise of the Greek city-states.

events.title: Neo-Assyrian Empire
events.descr: From the accession of Adad-nirari II, Assyria grows into the largest empire the world had yet seen, ruling from Assur, then Nimrud and Nineveh.

events.title: Sennacherib destroys Babylon
events.descr: After repeated Babylonian revolts, the Assyrian king besieges and destroys the city.

events.title: Nabopolassar crowned king of Babylon
events.descr: Nabopolassar revolts against Assyria, takes Babylon and Nippur and founds the Neo-Babylonian dynasty, allied with the Medes.

sources.sourceLocation: Foundation and the fall of Assyria (Lipschits 2005, pp. 13–14)

events.title: Medes sack Assur
events.descr: The old religious capital of Assyria falls to the Medes.

sources.sourceLocation: Foundation and the fall of Assyria

events.title: Fall of Nineveh
events.descr: Medes and Babylonians besiege Nineveh from May to August; king Sîn-šar-iškun dies and the Assyrian heartland collapses.

sources.sourceLocation: Account of the battle (Lipschits 2005, p. 18; ABC 3)

events.title: Fall of Harran: end of Assyria
events.descr: The last Assyrian king, Ashur-uballit II, is defeated at Harran.

events.title: Reign of Nebuchadnezzar II
events.descr: Babylon's greatest Neo-Babylonian king campaigns across the Levant and rebuilds Babylon on a grand scale.

events.title: Battle of Carchemish
events.descr: The Babylonians under crown prince Nebuchadnezzar defeat Egypt and the last Assyrian forces, taking control of Syria.

events.title: Babylon captures Jerusalem
events.descr: On 2 Adar (16 March 597 BCE) the city falls; King Jeconiah and the court are deported and Zedekiah is installed as a vassal.

events.title: Destruction of Jerusalem and the First Temple
events.descr: After Zedekiah's revolt, Babylon besieges Jerusalem from January 589, then burns the city and the First Temple and deports much of Judah's population.

events.title: Babylonian invasion of Egypt
events.descr: In the fourth year of Amasis, Babylon invades Egypt.

events.title: Cyrus revolts against Astyages
events.descr: Cyrus of Persia overthrows his Median overlord, the beginning of the Achaemenid Empire.

events.title: Reign of Nabonidus
events.descr: The last king of Babylon favours the moon god Sin and spends years in Arabia while his son Belshazzar governs.

events.title: Cyrus takes Babylon
events.descr: After victory at Opis, Persian forces enter Babylon on 12 October 539 BCE; Nabonidus surrenders and the Neo-Babylonian Empire ends.

events.title: Assur becomes an independent city-state
events.descr: Under Puzur-Ashur I, after the collapse of the Third Dynasty of Ur. One page credits independence to an earlier ruler, Ushpia, around 2090 BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: Under the Third Dynasty of Ur

source.sourceLocation: Under the Third Dynasty of Ur ('beginning with Ushpia c. 2090 BC')

events.title: Shamshi-Adad I conquers Assur
events.descr: An Amorite conqueror takes Assur and builds a kingdom across northern Mesopotamia, ruling from Shubat-Enlil. It falls apart soon after his death.

events.title: Assyria under Mitanni
events.descr: Assyria is a vassal of Mitanni for about 70 years, until it breaks free in the early 14th century.

events.title: Reign of Tukulti-Ninurta I
events.descr: The Middle Assyrian Empire at its height. He builds a new capital, Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta (c. 1233 BCE), and is assassinated about 1207 BCE.

events.title: Reign of Tiglath-Pileser I
events.descr: A second Middle Assyrian expansion after the decline of c. 1206–1115 BCE.

events.title: Ashurnasirpal II makes Nimrud (Kalhu) the capital
events.descr: Nimrud remains the capital until 706 BCE.

events.title: Reign of Tiglath-Pileser III
events.descr: Takes power in a revolt and turns Assyria into a far larger empire: he defeats Urartu (743), conquers Damascus (732) and Babylonia (729).

events.title: Sargon II moves the capital to Dur-Sharrukin
events.descr: The new city is the capital for only a year: after Sargon dies in battle in 705 BCE, Sennacherib moves the capital to Nineveh, where it stays until 612 BCE.

events.title: Reign of Ashurbanipal
events.descr: The last great Neo-Assyrian king. He wins a civil war against his brother Shamash-shum-ukin, king of Babylon (652–648), and destroys Elam. Assyria falls about two decades after his death.

events.title: Babylon revolts under Shamash-shum-ukin
events.descr: Ashurbanipal's brother, king of Babylon, rebels. He dies when Babylon falls after a siege in 648 BCE.

events.title: Tyre founded (by tradition)
events.descr: Herodotus' informants, the priests of Tyre, told him the city had been founded 2,300 years before his visit (around 450 BCE).

events.title: Proto-Sinaitic: the earliest alphabet
events.descr: Inscriptions from Sinai and Egypt adapting Egyptian hieroglyphs to write a Semitic language; the ancestor of the Phoenician alphabet. Scholars argue for an early date (around 1850 BCE) or a late one (around 1550 BCE).

events.title: Ebla first settled
events.descr: A small settlement in the Early Bronze Age that grows into a major Syrian city.

events.title: Ebla archives
events.descr: The age of the archives (Mardikh IIB1): cuneiform tablets in Sumerian and Eblaite, ending with the burning of palace G.

events.title: First destruction of Ebla
events.descr: Palace G burns. Who destroyed it is debated: suggestions include the Akkadian kings and, for the earlier dates, Eannatum or Lugalzagesi.

events.title: Mursili I destroys Ebla
events.descr: The Hittite king ends the third kingdom of Ebla, during the same campaigns that took Aleppo and Babylon.

events.title: Ugaritic alphabet
events.descr: A 30-letter alphabet written in cuneiform signs on clay. It falls out of use when Ugarit is destroyed.

events.title: Niqmaddu II: Ugarit becomes a Hittite vassal
events.descr: Ugarit, which had corresponded with Egypt in the Amarna letters, passes into the Hittite sphere.

events.title: Ugarit destroyed
events.descr: Destroyed during the Late Bronze Age collapse, in the reign of its last king, Ammurapi.

events.title: Phoenician alphabet
events.descr: A 22-letter consonantal alphabet, ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Aramaic and Hebrew scripts. 1050 BCE is the conventional date; arrowheads from c. 1100 BCE carry early examples.

events.title: Hiram I: Tyre becomes the leading Phoenician city
events.descr: Tyre becomes the dominant city-state under Hiram I.

events.title: Carthage founded
events.descr: Tyrian colonists found Carthage in North Africa; in Roman accounts, led by Dido.

events.title: Tyre under Babylonian rule
events.descr: Tyre comes under Neo-Babylonian rule.

events.title: Alexander the Great takes Tyre
events.descr: After a siege during which he builds a causeway to the island city. Eight thousand Tyrians die and 30,000 are sold into slavery.

events.title: Merneptah Stele names "Israel"
events.descr: Carved in Merneptah's fifth year, it lists Ashkelon, Gezer, Yanoam and Israel among the defeated: the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible.

events.title: Kingdom of Israel (Samaria)
events.descr: The northern kingdom, from Jeroboam I to Hoshea. Its capital moves from Shechem and Tirzah to Samaria (from c. 880 BCE).

events.title: Kingdom of Judah
events.descr: The southern kingdom, ruled by the House of David from Jerusalem, from Rehoboam to Zedekiah.

events.title: Assyria conquers Israel
events.descr: The Neo-Assyrian Empire ends the northern kingdom after campaigns from 732 BCE; Sargon II deports 27,290 Israelites.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Conquest by the Neo-Assyrian Empire (732–720 BCE)

events.title: Philistines settle in Canaan
events.descr: Amid the Late Bronze Age collapse. Typically Philistine artifacts appear in Canaan in the 12th century; the link to the Sea Peoples Ramesses III fought is a hypothesis.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar II destroys the Philistine cities
events.descr: After a revolt, Babylon destroys Ashkelon, Gaza, Aphek and Ekron and deports their people.

events.title: Reign of Hazael of Damascus
events.descr: A usurper who fights the Assyrians and conquers Israel.

events.title: Tiglath-Pileser III conquers Damascus
events.descr: Assyria annexes Aram-Damascus and executes its last king, Rezin.

events.title: Susa founded
events.descr: The settlement that becomes the chief city of Elam.

events.title: Linear Elamite script
events.descr: A script for the Elamite language, associated with Puzur-Inshushinak (in power around 2150 BCE). Its decipherment was proposed in 2020–2022.

events.title: Untash-Napirisha builds the ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil
events.descr: A temple complex near Susa. Construction was sometime in the 14th or 13th century BCE; 1250 is the conventional date.

events.title: Ashurbanipal sacks Susa
events.descr: Assyria's final campaigns against Elam destroy Susa and Chogha Zanbil (the latter 'about 645 BC').

events.title: Medes first appear in Assyrian records
events.descr: Shalmaneser III sends a sortie against four settlements, one identified as Media. Medes appear in Assyrian texts from the 9th century BCE.

events.title: Mannaea first mentioned
events.descr: An inscription from Shalmaneser III's 30th year names Mannaea and its ruler Udaki.

events.title: Medes annex Mannaea
events.descr: Mannaea is absorbed into the Median kingdom by the late 7th century BCE.

events.title: Tiglath-Pileser III defeats Sarduri II of Urartu
events.descr: Urartu had beaten Assyria at Arpad in 754 BCE; this victory reverses the balance.

events.title: Reign of Darius the Great
events.descr: The empire's campaigns fail to conquer Scythia (513) and Greece (492–490).

events.title: Greco-Persian Wars
events.descr: From the Ionian Revolt to the end of hostilities; Persian invasions of Greece are repulsed in 492–490 and 480–479 BCE.

events.title: Alexander conquers the Achaemenid Empire
events.descr: The end of a Macedonian campaign that began in 336 BCE.

events.title: Dilmun at its height
events.descr: A trading centre in Bahrain, between Mesopotamia and the Indus, prosperous in the first centuries of the 2nd millennium BCE, then declining from around 1720.

events.title: Last mention of Dilmun
events.descr: Neo-Babylonian records; after the fall of Babylon the name falls out of use.

events.title: Ravi (Hakra) phase at Harappa
events.descr: The first settlement at Harappa. A 2025 study dates its start as early as about 3700 BCE.

events.title: Kot Diji phase
events.descr: The last Early Harappan phase before the cities.

events.title: Indus script
events.descr: Short inscriptions on seals and pottery; still undeciphered. A possible proto-script dates from c. 3500 BCE, and rare later graffiti until c. 1300 BCE.

events.title: Mohenjo-daro
events.descr: A major city of the Mature Harappan phase, abandoned c. 1700 BCE along with the other large Indus cities.

events.title: Dholavira
events.descr: A walled city in Kutch with elaborate water reservoirs. Recent radiocarbon dating puts its first stage around 3500 BCE; after a desertion it was reoccupied until c. 1450 BCE.

source.sourceLocation: Timeline ('recent C14 datings': Stage I c. 3500-3200 BCE)

events.title: Lothal
events.descr: A Harappan port town in Gujarat. A massive flood around 1900 BCE destroyed it.

events.title: Ships from Meluhha in Akkad
events.descr: Sargon of Akkad mentions ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun. Most scholars identify Meluhha with the Indus Valley.

events.title: Indus seal impression at Susa
events.descr: A cylinder-seal impression with Indus characters, found in a stratum at Susa: evidence of Indus–Mesopotamian contact.

events.title: Mehrgarh abandoned
events.descr: One of the earliest farming sites in South Asia (from c. 5250 or 7000 BCE) is largely abandoned sometime between 2600 and 2000 BCE.

events.title: Last Mesopotamian mention of Meluhha
events.descr: Direct trade had already given way to trade through Dilmun, possibly as the Indus cities declined.

sources.sourceLocation: Trading colony ('no known mentions of Meluhha after 1760 BCE')

events.title: Liangzhu culture disappears
events.descr: The jade-working culture of the Yangtze Delta, which flourished around 2500 BCE with a 290-hectare walled city, vanishes after a wet period, perhaps linked to the 4.2-kiloyear climate event.

events.title: Walled city built at Yanshi
events.descr: Near Erlitou. The Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project treats it as the founding of the Shang.

events.title: Pan Geng moves the Shang capital to Yin (Anyang)
events.descr: The page dates this to the beginning of the 14th century BCE. Yin serves twelve kings until the Zhou conquest.

events.title: Reign of Wu Ding
events.descr: The Shang at its zenith. The oldest oracle-bone inscriptions date from his reign.

events.title: Oracle-bone inscriptions
events.descr: Divination records on bones and shells from Yin: the earliest known Chinese writing. No identifiable writing before the 13th century BCE has been found.

events.title: Battle of Muye: Zhou conquers Shang
events.descr: King Wu of Zhou defeats Di Xin, the last Shang king. The day and month are certain but the year is not: at least 44 dates have been proposed.

source.sourceLocation: Dating (a reading of the Li gui inscription)
Dating ('44 different dates … ranging from 1130 to 1018 BC')

events.title: Walled city at Sanxingdui
events.descr: A Bronze Age culture in Sichuan with no written records, famous for large bronze heads and masks (13th–12th century BCE).

events.title: Gonghe Regency
events.descr: The earliest securely dated event in Chinese history.

events.title: Zhou capital moves east
events.descr: After the disaster at Mount Li, the court moves to Wangcheng: the end of the Western Zhou.

events.title: Spring and Autumn period
events.descr: The first part of the Eastern Zhou.

events.title: Warring States period
events.descr: Qin deposes the last Zhou king in 256 BCE and unifies China in 221 BCE.

events.title: Watson Brake mounds
events.descr: An earthwork complex in Louisiana, built over about 500 years and abandoned around 2800 BCE: far older than Poverty Point, once thought the earliest mound site in North America.

events.title: Poverty Point
events.descr: Monumental earthworks in Louisiana: six concentric ridges (mostly built 1600–1300 BCE) and large mounds. Recent syntheses put construction from as early as 1800 to as late as 1200 BCE.

events.title: Caral
events.descr: The best-known city of the Caral–Supe civilization. Its abandonment has been linked to a prolonged drought around 2200 BCE.

source.sourceLocation: History and geography (Shady: 'habitation from 2627 BCE to 2020 BCE')

events.title: Caral flutes
events.descr: Bone flutes, the only find at Caral with a stated radiocarbon margin.

events.title: Valdivia pottery
events.descr: Phase A on the coast of Ecuador, long thought the oldest pottery in South America.

events.title: San Lorenzo, the first Olmec centre
events.descr: The largest city in Mesoamerica from roughly 1200 to 900 BCE, known for its colossal stone heads. Destroyed in the 10th century BCE.

events.title: La Venta
events.descr: The main Olmec centre after San Lorenzo, with a great earthen pyramid; all but abandoned by the beginning of the 4th century BCE.

events.title: La Venta Great Pyramid
events.descr: A radiocarbon date from Complex C, the great pyramid.

events.title: First Maya cities
events.descr: The first Maya cities develop in the Preclassic period.

events.title: El Mirador
events.descr: A Preclassic Maya city in the Mirador Basin, at its height from the 3rd century BCE.

source.sourceLocation: History ('from about the 6th century BC'): start of century

events.title: Earliest Maya writing
events.descr: The earliest inscriptions in an identifiably Maya script, in the Petén Basin.

events.title: Chavín de Huántar: Old Temple
events.descr: The highland ceremonial centre of the Chavín culture; the New Temple follows from about 500 to 200 BCE.

events.title: Megalithic temples of Malta
events.descr: Temple complexes built in three phases (Ġgantija, Saflieni, Tarxien). Tarxien remained in use until 2500 BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Temple phases ('Based on recalibrated radiocarbon dating')

events.title: Ötzi the Iceman dies in the Alps
events.descr: A Copper Age man, about 45 years old when he died. His body was discovered in 1991.

events.title: Newgrange passage tomb
events.descr: A Neolithic monument, about 500 years older than the current form of Stonehenge. Its first period of use lasted around 1,000 years.

source.sourceLocation: Construction ('Some put its period of construction … at 3000 to 2500 BC')

events.title: Stonehenge begun
events.descr: The first stage, an earthwork. Building continued in phases until about 1600 BCE.

events.title: Stonehenge: the sarsen circle raised
events.descr: The great sarsen stones are placed; the bluestones follow between 2400 and 2200 BCE (radiocarbon).

events.title: Nebra sky disc
events.descr: Associated with the Bornhöck mound (c. 1800 BCE), an Únětice princely grave.

sources.sourceLocation: History of research (caption 'Early Bronze Age, 1800–1600 BC') and Barrows

events.title: Kivik 'King's Grave'
events.descr: A Bronze Age burial.

events.title: Wehringen cart grave
events.descr: A cart burial, one of the few Hallstatt finds with a 'solid dating'.

events.title: Founding of Rome (traditional)
events.descr: Legend credits Romulus. Varro's 753 BCE became the basis of the Roman calendar; ancient writers disagreed, and most modern historians treat the accounts as fiction. Archaeologically, hilltop villages united by the later 8th century BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Ancient tradition, Chronological disagreements, Archaeology

events.title: Monarchy overthrown: the Roman Republic
events.descr: By tradition the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, is expelled and the first consuls are elected.

events.title: Gauls defeat Rome at the Allia and sack the city
events.descr: Celts under Brennus defeat the Romans and sack Rome. The traditional (Varronian) date is 390 BCE; modern historians consider c. 387 the most probable.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox and Date of the battle

source.sourceLocation: Date of the battle (Polybius; most probable)

events.title: Latin League dissolved
events.descr: The league of Latin cities is dissolved.

events.title: Greek alphabet
events.descr: In use since the late 9th or early 8th century BCE; still used today.

events.title: First Olympic Games (traditional)
events.descr: Traditionally dated to 776 BCE (Aristotle); an Olympiad count gives 765, and scholars disagree on when the games began.

events.title: Greek colonisation
events.descr: Greek cities found colonies abroad, particularly in the 8th–6th centuries BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and map caption ('Archaic period: 750–550 BC')

events.title: Solon reforms Athens
events.descr: Solon is appointed 'archon and mediator' in 594/3 BCE.

events.title: Cleisthenes' reforms in Athens
events.descr: After the fall of the last Athenian tyrant (510 BCE). Classical Greece calls it the first significant event of the 5th century.

source.sourceLocation: 5th century BC ('the first significant event … in 508 BC')
Background ('Cleisthenes was thus restored to Athens (507 BC)')

events.title: Battle of Marathon
events.descr: The Persians are defeated in their first invasion of Greece.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.descr: A naval battle during Xerxes' invasion of Greece (481–479 BCE).

events.title: Peloponnesian War
events.descr: Athens and Sparta fight for hegemony over Greece; Persia backs Sparta from 413 and Athens surrenders in 404.

events.title: Reign of Philip II of Macedon
events.descr: King of Macedon from 359 BCE. He is assassinated in 336 and immediately succeeded by his son Alexander.

events.title: Philip II wins the Battle of Chaeronea
events.descr: The next year (337 BCE) Philip becomes hegemon of the Hellenic League.

events.title: Early Cycladic culture
events.descr: The island culture of the Cyclades evolves in three Early Cycladic phases, then shades into the archaeologically murkier Middle Cycladic around 2000 BCE.

events.title: Macedon moves its capital from Aigai to Pella
events.descr: Pella remains the capital until the kingdom ends in 168 BCE.

events.title: Reign of Midas of Phrygia
events.descr: The historical king behind the legends, whom most historians identify with Mita. Ancient writers date his death to around 695 (Eusebius) or 676 BCE (Julius Africanus).

events.title: Cimmerians destroy the kingdom of Phrygia
events.descr: The end of the major power in Anatolia before Lydia.

events.title: Cimmerians sack Sardis; Gyges killed
events.descr: The third Cimmerian attack on Lydia.

events.title: Lydian coins
events.descr: Electrum coins from Lydia, among the oldest in existence.

sources.sourceLocation: lead ('dated to around the 7th century BC')

source.sourceLocation: lead ('around the 7th century BC'): start of century

events.title: Reign of Croesus
events.descr: The last king of Lydia. After Cyrus conquers the Medes (550 BCE), Croesus attacks Persia and loses his kingdom.

events.title: Cyrus conquers Lydia
events.descr: Lydia becomes a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire.

events.title: Thutmose III subjugates Cyprus
events.descr: Egypt claims Cyprus; the Hittites replace Egypt there in the 13th century BCE.

events.title: Alashiya submits to the Hittites
events.descr: Shortly before the Late Bronze Age collapse, Tudḫaliya IV and Šuppiluliuma II force Alashiya's king to sign a treaty of submission. Alashiya was a major source of copper for the Near East.

events.title: Ten Cypriot kingdoms under Assyria
events.descr: Esarhaddon's prism lists ten city-kingdoms of Cyprus. Assyrian rule ends with the fall of the Neo-Assyrian Empire (609 BCE).

sources.sourceLocation: Assyrian conquest and the ten city-kingdoms

events.title: Amasis II of Egypt conquers Cyprus
Persia conquers Cyprus
events.descr: The Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great takes Cyprus.

events.title: Terramare culture collapses
events.descr: The Bronze Age Terramare culture enters a severe crisis around 1200 BCE and collapses about 1150.

events.title: Samnite Wars
events.descr: Three wars (343–341, 327–304, 298–290 BCE) in which Rome subjugates the Samnites, despite their great victory at the Caudine Forks (321).

events.title: Teres I founds the Odrysian kingdom
events.descr: A Thracian kingdom founded after the failed Persian invasion of Greece. Philip II of Macedon conquers it in 340 BCE; Seuthes III revives it around 330.

events.title: Carthage independent of Tyre
events.descr: Independence from its mother city, Tyre.

events.title: Battle of Alalia
events.descr: Etruscans and Carthaginians join forces against the Greeks, containing Greek expansion in Spain.

source.sourceLocation: infobox ('Some time between 540 BC and 535 BC')

events.title: Sicilian Wars
events.descr: Carthage and the Greek cities of Sicily fight for the island, from the first recorded clash (580) until the Punic Wars. Carthage keeps the west, the Greeks the east.

events.title: Battle of Himera
events.descr: The Greeks of Sicily defeat Hamilcar's expedition, crippling Carthage's power on the island for decades. Tradition put it on the same day as Salamis; modern scholars reject that.

events.title: Cumae founded
events.descr: A colony of Chalkis and Eretria in Italy.

events.title: Syracuse founded
events.descr: Founded by Greek colonists from Corinth. Thucydides' 733 is considered the most reliable date.

events.title: Sybaris destroyed
events.descr: The Greek city of Sybaris, prosperous from 600 BCE, is destroyed.

events.title: Athenian expedition to Sicily
events.descr: Athens attacks Syracuse during the Peloponnesian War; the expedition is destroyed in 413 BCE.

events.title: Nuraghe towers built
events.descr: Sardinia's nuraghe towers, built in large numbers from about 1800 BCE; construction had stopped by the 12th–11th century BCE.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('already stopped by the 12th–11th century BC')

events.title: Talaiotic culture at its height
events.descr: The era of the talayots on Menorca and Mallorca. Decline sets in between 600 and 500 BCE, with the onset of Punic influence.

sources.sourceLocation: Funerary spaces ('maximum splendor … from 850-800 BCE to 500 BCE') and The Talayot

events.title: Tartessos: the Orientalizing phase
events.descr: The height of Tartessian metalwork in southern Iberia, before it gave way to the Classic Iberian culture.

events.title: Libu and Sea Peoples invade Egypt
events.descr: In Merneptah's 5th year a Libyan coalition under Meryey, allied with Sea Peoples, is defeated.

events.title: Cyrene founded
events.descr: Colonists from Thera led by Battus I found Cyrene, by Greek tradition in 631 BCE; archaeology puts Greek settlement in the mid-7th century.

events.title: Cyrene defeats Egypt at Irasa
events.descr: The pharaoh Apries, called in by Adicran, is defeated at Irasa.

events.title: Persians sack Barca
events.descr: The Persian governor of Egypt, Aryandes, besieges and sacks the Cyrenaican city of Barca.

events.title: Botai people herd horses
events.descr: The Botai are major users of horses by about 3500 BCE. Genetics shows Przewalski's horses descend from Botai herds, while modern domestic horses are not closely related to them.

events.title: Steppe herders migrate to the Altai
events.descr: People from the pre-Yamnaya Repin culture cross the Eurasian steppe to the Altai, founding the Afanasievo culture, which has been linked to the Proto-Tocharian language. The two populations are genetically indistinguishable.

source.sourceLocation: Genetics map caption ('3000 BC: Initial eastward migration')

events.title: Yamnaya spreads across the Pontic–Caspian steppe
events.descr: Herders with two-wheeled carts and four-wheeled wagons. Later Corded Ware, Bell Beaker, Sintashta and Andronovo populations derive large parts of their ancestry from the Yamnaya.

events.title: Yamnaya expansion into the Danube valley
Yamnaya transforms into Corded Ware
events.descr: In the north, the Corded Ware culture follows the Yamnaya and carries much of its ancestry; how directly one descends from the other is debated. The same map dates the end of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture to c. 2700 BCE.

events.title: The modern domestic horse emerges
events.descr: Genomes trace the lineage of all modern domestic horses (DOM2) to the Volga–Don region around 2200 BCE. Its spread is linked with the peoples before Sintashta, and these horses are buried in Sintashta kurgans with early chariots.

source.sourceLocation: lead ('around 2200 BCE in the Volga–Don region')
lead (Taylor: 'true domestication did not take place until around 2000 BCE')

events.title: Arkaim, a fortified Sintashta settlement
events.descr: A settlement of the Sintashta culture, attributed to early Proto-Indo-Iranian speakers. Discovered in 1987.

events.title: The oldest known chariots
events.descr: Spoke-wheeled vehicles buried with horses in Sintashta graves. Some scholars class them as carts rather than true chariots. Chariots appear on seals at Kültepe in Anatolia by about 1900 BCE, reach Egypt around 1650 BCE and are heavily used by the Mycenaeans around 1600 BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Origins, Near East and Greece

events.title: Indo-Aryan migrations begin
events.descr: The Indo-Aryans split from the Indo-Iranians of the Sintashta and Andronovo cultures and migrate south, by way of the Bactria–Margiana culture, into northern Syria and the Punjab. In South Asia it begins as a slow diffusion in the Late Harappan period. Indo-Iranian loan words appear in Hurrian treaties of Mitanni in the mid-second millennium.

events.title: Srubnaya replaces the Lola culture
events.descr: The Timber-grave culture, probably Iranian-speaking, takes over the Lola lands; historical sources say the Scythians later succeeded it.

events.title: Death of the Cimmerian king Dugdammî
events.descr: Dugdammî, who led the attack on Lydia, kills himself in Cilicia.

events.title: Scythians and Lydians defeat the Cimmerians
events.descr: Madyes's Scythians and the Lydians under Alyattes defeat the Cimmerians and Treres; Herodotus and Polyaenus say permanently.

events.title: Madyes: Scythian rule over Media
events.descr: King of the Scythians (c. 658/9–625 BCE). Helping Ashurbanipal suppress the revolt of 652 BCE, he invades Media and holds it for the Assyrians for twenty-eight years, until Cyaxares invites the Scythian rulers to a banquet in 625 BCE and murders them.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, Conquest of Media and Revolt of Media and death

events.title: Medes expel the Scythians from West Asia
events.descr: The Scythians retreat into the Pontic steppe.

events.title: Darius I's Scythian campaign
events.descr: Darius crosses the Bosphorus on a bridge of boats and then the Danube. The Persians damage the Scythians but suffer heavy losses; the page calls it little more than an expensive stalemate.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead, The campaign and Aftermath

events.title: Philip II defeats Ateas
events.descr: The Scythian king Ateas is killed in battle against Philip II of Macedon in Dobruja, and his empire falls to pieces.

events.title: Arzhan 1 kurgan
events.descr: An early Saka burial mound.

events.title: Tomyris of the Massagetae kills Cyrus the Great
events.descr: Cyrus dies in battle against the Massagetae, led by their queen Tomyris. Ctesias tells another version, in which he dies fighting the Derbices.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Death of Cyrus and Aftermath

events.title: Pazyryk burials
events.descr: Burials at Pazyryk and neighbouring sites in the Altai. A Saka (eastern Scythian) culture.

source.sourceLocation: Archaeology ('5th century BC'): start of century

events.title: A-Group culture at its height
events.descr: The first powerful society in Nubia, with commercial ties to Egypt. Agriculture first appears in the Terminal A-Group period (c. 3200–3000 BCE).

events.title: An early pharaoh defeats the A-Group
events.descr: The relief of Gebel Sheikh Suleiman likely shows an early pharaoh, possibly Djer, victorious over A-Group Nubians. One account has the First Dynasty destroying the A-Group around 3100 BCE.

events.title: Early C-Group culture appears in Lower Nubia

sources.sourceLocation: History > Early Kerma ('By 2300 BC, the Early C-Group culture was also appearing in Lower Nubia')

events.title: Senusret III fortifies Buhen
events.descr: Senusret III campaigns four times into Kush and builds a line of forts within signalling distance of one another; Buhen, below the Second Cataract, is the northernmost.

events.title: Classic Kerma: the kingdom at its peak
events.descr: Contemporary with the Second Intermediate Period. At its zenith Kerma partners with the Hyksos against Egypt.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Site and periodisation and Classic Kerma

source.sourceLocation: lead ('latest phase, lasting from about 1700 to 1500 BC')

events.title: Kushites capture Buhen
events.descr: The fortress falls to the Kushites during the 13th Dynasty; Ahmose I retakes it at the start of the 18th.

sources.sourceLocation: Fortress and The Buhen Horse ('initial sacking … circa 1675 BC')

events.title: Kerma invades deep into Egypt
events.descr: Recorded in the tomb of Sobeknakht II.

events.title: Thutmose I conquers Kush and destroys Kerma
events.descr: Egypt annexes Nubia and Thutmose I builds a fortress at Tombos near the Third Cataract. Nubian rebellions continue for about 220 years.

source.sourceLocation: Late Kerma ('annexation of Nubia … c. 1504 BC')

events.title: Kush becomes independent, centred at Napata
events.descr: As the New Kingdom disintegrates, Kush becomes an independent kingdom, possibly a successor of Kerma.

events.title: Alara, first Kushite king known by name
Piye conquers Egypt
events.descr: In his twentieth year the Kushite king Piye invades against Tefnakht of Sais, wins at Herakleopolis and takes Hermopolis after a five-month siege. He then returns to Napata and never comes back to Egypt.

events.title: Reign of Taharqa
events.descr: The 25th Dynasty's best-known king. He defeats the Assyrians in 674 BCE but loses Memphis to Esarhaddon in 671, retakes it in 669, and dies in 664. The Kush page says he died at Napata, the Taharqa page at Thebes.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox, lead and War between Taharqa and Assyria

events.title: Psamtik II sacks Napata
events.descr: The Egyptian army fights its way to Pnubs (Kerma) and Napata, which is sacked under the Kushite king Aspelta.

source.sourceLocation: Campaigns and battles ('a foray into Nubia in 592 BC')

events.title: Kush moves its capital to Meroë
events.descr: Aspelta moves the capital far south of Napata, just after the Egyptian sack. The royal burial ground follows only around 280 BCE, and the main temple of Amun stays at Napata.

sources.sourceLocation: infobox and Meroitic period ('possibly c. 591 BC')

events.title: First recorded expedition to Punt
events.descr: Organised by Sahure of the Fifth Dynasty. Recent evidence places Punt in northwestern Eritrea.

sources.sourceLocation: lead and Egyptian expeditions to Punt

events.title: Hannu sails to Punt
events.descr: An officer of Mentuhotep III (11th Dynasty) organises one or more voyages to Punt.

events.title: Earliest known king of Dʿmt
events.descr: A contemporary of the Sabaean ruler Karib'il Watar. Dʿmt was an Ethio-Sabaean kingdom, its capital probably Yeha, where the temple of Ilmuqah still stands.

events.title: Millet domesticated at Tichitt
events.descr: The crop was fully domesticated by 1100 BCE at the latest. Plateau settlements are built from about 1400 BCE.

events.title: Classic Tichitt
events.descr: Pastoralists and farmers on the cliffs of Dhar Tichitt; they are thought to be ancestors of the Soninke. The chronology is contentious.

events.title: Nok terracotta sculptures
events.descr: The earliest Nok terracottas may date from about 900 BCE. The Middle Nok period (c. 900–300 BCE) sees a dramatic increase in sites, terracotta fragments and iron objects.

events.title: Iron smelting in the Nok culture
events.descr: Iron metallurgy may have developed independently here.

source.sourceLocation: Iron metallurgy ('in the 9th century BCE or 8th century BCE')

events.title: Bantu languages split into East and West
events.descr: The expansion most likely began in the highlands between Cameroon and Nigeria.

events.title: Bantu speakers reach Lake Victoria and Angola
events.descr: The Western Stream reaches the southern edge of the rainforest and central Angola; the Eastern Stream, with Urewe pottery and one of the oldest iron-smelting centres in Africa, reaches west of Lake Victoria.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Western Stream and Eastern Stream

events.title: Herodotus describes the Garamantes
events.descr: The earliest written record of them: "a very great nation" who herded cattle and farmed dates.

source.sourceLocation: History ('5th century BC'): start of century

events.title: The Rigveda composed
events.descr: Usually dated to roughly 1500–1000 BCE; the dates are not confirmed and remain contentious. Codified around 1200–1000 BCE in the early Kuru kingdom (Witzel).

source.sourceLocation: lead ('a wider approximation of c. 1900–1200 BCE')

events.title: Vedic culture spreads to the Ganges plain
events.descr: After 1000 BCE iron axes and ploughs come into wide use.

events.title: The sixteen Mahajanapadas
events.descr: Political units consolidate into large kingdoms during the second urbanisation; Magadha wins the struggle for supremacy that follows.

events.title: Persia conquers the Indus valley
events.descr: Cyrus the Great begins the campaign around 535 BCE; Darius I pushes into the Indus valley around 518, up to the Jhelum. Gandhara and Hindush become Persian provinces; Kamboja and Gandhara form the twentieth and richest satrapy.

events.title: Reign of Bimbisara of Magadha
events.descr: The Haryanka king annexes Anga; his son Ajatashatru succeeds him (by Buddhist accounts, by killing him). Under the short chronology he reigns c. 457–405 BCE.

events.title: Life of Mahavira
events.descr: Traditional dates; historians place him in the 6th or 5th century BCE, a contemporary of the Buddha under Bimbisara and Ajatashatru.

events.title: Life of the Buddha
events.descr: He lives under Bimbisara and dies under Ajatashatru. Most scholars who give a date place his death within 20 years of 400 BCE; earlier scholarship used 563–483 BCE.

source.sourceLocation: infobox and Dating ('the earlier dates of 563–483 BCE')
infobox and Dating ('within 20 years either side of 400 BCE')

events.title: The Nanda dynasty takes Magadha
events.descr: The Nandas usurp the Shishunaga throne; Chandragupta Maurya overthrows them.

events.title: Bronze working at Ban Chiang
events.descr: Crucibles and bronze fragments; the chronology is still in considerable dispute (Higham puts settlement about 1500 BCE and the Bronze Age about 1000). Rice phytoliths from the lowest grave give 2100 BCE.

events.title: Rice farming reaches the Red River
events.descr: Introduced in the Phùng Nguyên period, according to the page by northern Dai people (a cited study says from southern China).

events.title: Đông Sơn bronze drums
events.descr: Produced from about 600 BCE or earlier until the third century CE, and found from eastern Indonesia to Vietnam and southern China. Vietnamese historians attribute the culture to the states of Văn Lang and Âu Lạc.

events.title: Sa Huỳnh–Kalanay trade network
events.descr: A trade sphere reaching Taiwan, southern Thailand, Borneo and the Philippines. The Sa Huỳnh, who buried their cremated dead in lidded jars, were most likely predecessors of the Austronesian-speaking Cham.

events.title: Traditional founding of the Hùng kings
events.descr: In legend Lộc Tục comes to power in 2879 BCE; Văn Lang ends when Thục Phán overthrows the last Hùng king, about 258 BCE. The dating of events is still a subject of research.

sources.sourceLocation: lead, Xích Quỷ Kingdom, Chronology and Âu Lạc Kingdom

events.title: Stone jars placed on the Plain of Jars
events.descr: Luminescence dating puts the jars in place as early as 1240–660 BCE; Madeleine Colani concluded in 1930 that they were associated with burial practices.

events.title: Sannai-Maruyama, a large Jōmon settlement
events.descr: Hunter-gatherers use the site from around 3900 BCE and settle permanently around 2900; a six-pillar building stands by about 2600. The settlement ends around 2300 BCE.

events.title: Traditional founding of Old Chosŏn by Tan’gun
events.descr: The mythological founding date from the Samguk yusa. Chinese records treat Old Chosŏn as a country only from 195 BCE; it falls to the Han in 108 BCE.

events.title: Rice farming and dolmens in Korea
events.descr: In the Early Mumun, rice agriculture appears beside the earlier millet farming, and megalithic burials begin.

events.title: Middle Mumun: paddy rice (Songguk-ri culture)
events.descr: Wet-field rice farming in southern Korea; the culture reaches Jeju Island and western Japan.

events.title: Korean rice farmers settle in Kyushu
events.descr: Korean-type settlements appear in western Kyushu, bringing wet rice farming and bronze and iron metallurgy; Yayoi-style pottery appears in northern Kyushu by 800 BCE. Jōmon and Yayoi ways of life coexist for around a thousand years.

sources.sourceLocation: Late and Final Jōmon and Chronology

events.title: Traditional founding of Japan by Emperor Jimmu
events.descr: The founding date given by the Nihon Shoki, a foundation narrative rather than history.
